name: Sabar Drum
description: The sabar is the single-headed drum at the heart of Wolof and Serer music in Senegal, its goatskin head lashed to a carved wooden body with a signature system of lacing and seven pegs. Woodworkers of the lawbe caste carve the shell from baobab or dimb trunks, while griot percussionists of the gewel caste build, tune, and play the drum with one bare hand and a curved stick. Sabar rhythms are named, and older players say 'the sabar can speak': bakks, rhythmic phrases matched to spoken Wolof, were traditionally used to announce news, praise people, and summon the community. The drums anchor baptisms, weddings, and circumcisions, and every wrestler in the popular Lamb contests fields his own drumming group, whose rivalry is nearly as intense as the bout itself. Largely male through most of its history, sabar playing has opened to women and been carried worldwide by masters such as Doudou N'Diaye Rose, while its rhythms live on in the pop genre mbalax. Making a drum is itself touched by belief, for spirits (jinne) are said to dwell in certain trees, and watching a new head being fitted is held to bring good luck.

name: Xalam Lute
material: Wood, skin, gut or nylon strings
description: The xalam is a plucked five-string lute of the Wolof of Senegal, with a calabash or carved wooden bowl body, a skin head, and strings grouped into two melody and three rhythm strings. Played by griots (gewel), it produces the interlocking lines that back praise-songs, genealogies, and narrative epics, and its twanging rhythms support both festive dance music and the serious recitation of lineage history. Across the Sahel the same instrument appears under other names, such as the hoddu of the Fulani and the khalam, with each people tuning and playing it in its own idiom. A griot's xalam was far more than entertainment: the words carried by the strings could flatter, mock, or counsel, making the instrument the audible badge of the praise-singer's craft. Older songs survive within griot families, while contemporary musicians have carried the xalam onto popular stages, keeping the sound of praise orature alive in Senegal and the diaspora.

name: Dan Mask
description: The dan mask is a carved wooden face mask of the Dan people of western Ivory Coast, admired for its smooth, polished surface, narrow eye slits, and the fine balance of its features. Each mask is inhabited by a spirit called gle, and the wearer becomes that spirit during the dance, so the mask is handled with ritual care: it is oiled, fed, and hidden from profane eyes when not in use. Masks take many characters, from the playful entertainment mask to the warrior mask and the judge that fines wrongdoers in village disputes, and the same basic form was adopted by the neighbouring We and Guro peoples. Some masks belong to whole communities or age sets, while others pass through family lines, and their guardianship is a position of real responsibility. European and American collectors prized dan masks in the twentieth century for their serene, 'classical' faces, and the form had a marked influence on modernist sculpture.

name: Baule Goli Mask
description: The goli is a round-faced, painted mask of the Baule people of the Ivory Coast, worn with a full costume during village celebrations, funerals, and the dances of the goli society. The word names a whole sequence of masks that appear in a fixed order, from the round kpan faces through animal forms to the large, frightening figured masks, a progression that retraces the Baule cosmos and the order of communal life. Male and female variants dance in pairs, and the female face, with its calm forehead and scarified temples, is regarded as the model of Baule beauty. The dance is closely tied to the goli spirit powers believed to enter the masked dancers, and the performances draw the entire village together at moments of joy and mourning. In Baule belief the mask is not decoration but a doorway for those powers, which is why its storage and handling follow strict tradition.

name: Tuareg Takuba Sword
description: The takuba is the straight-bladed sword of the Tuareg of the Sahara and Sahel, a double-edged blade of about a metre with a deep crossguard and a flat metal pommel. Because Tuareg custom regards iron as unclean, the guard and grip are covered with tooled leather, and the scabbard is worked with stamped and pierced designs that reflect the wealth and rank of its owner. Swords were made and mounted by the inadan (blacksmith) caste, who spoke their own secret language and were credited with magical power over metal. Given to a young man as he came of age, the takuba marked nobility and courage, and it was carried in raids, duels, and the caravan wars of the desert until firearms displaced it. Many blades came from European or Arab forges and were remounted in Sahelian style, evidence of a long trade across the Sahara. Today the takuba is worn at festivals and ceremonies as a badge of Tuareg identity and honour.

name: Agadez Cross Pendant
powers: Worn as a protective amulet, with the arms said to guard the wearer in life's directions.
description: The Agadez cross, or tanaghilt, is the best-known of the Tuareg silver pendants of Niger, a cruciform amulet with four or more arms radiating from a central square, traditionally cast by the smiths (inadan) of Agadez. Agadez and the wider Air region have their own named cross designs, and the form is sometimes said to be a stylised map, a key, or the four directions that guard the wearer on the paths of life. The pendant is given at the passages of life, at a birth, a naming, an initiation, or a marriage, and it is worn by both men and women as a protective amulet, especially in the desert, where silver is believed to bring safety and luck. Older pieces are worked in silver and niello, while modern crosses are also cast in gold for the jewellery trade. Beyond Niger, the Agadez cross has become an emblem of Tuareg culture worldwide, appearing on flags and in the tourist crafts of the Sahara even as the full meaning of the form remains a matter of oral tradition.

name: Sao Bronze Bracelet
description: The bronze and copper ornaments of the Sao people come from the mound sites of the Lake Chad basin, where a succession of urbanised societies flourished from around the sixth century BC to the fifteenth century AD. Excavations at towns like Mdaga and the islands of the Chari and Logone rivers have yielded bracelets, anklets, pendants, and small anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figurines cast by the lost-wax method. The careful casting of rings and armlets shows a metalworking tradition of real technical skill, and the spread of finds hints at long-distance trade in metal along the Sahel. The modern populations of the region remember the Sao in legend as giants and founders of vanished cities, so the bracelets bind living folklore to the archaeological record. Major collections are preserved at the National Museum in N'Djamena, and the objects remain key evidence of early Central African metallurgy.
source: Sao archaeological finds; National Museum of N'Djamena

name: Bamum Beaded Throne (Mandu Yenu)
description: The Mandu Yenu is the royal throne of the Bamum kingdom of the Cameroon Grassfields, a carved wooden stool and footstool completely encased in glass beads, cowrie shells, and brass studs. Mandu Yenu means 'rich in beads', and the most famous example, made for the Bamum court in the nineteenth century, was given by King Njoya to the German Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1908 and now rests in Berlin; a near-identical copy he commissioned remains in the palace at Foumban. The carving carries royal symbols such as the two-headed snake and the spider of wisdom, while two large figures, the protective twins Mandu and Yenu, stand behind the seat, and smaller rifle-bearing figures on the footrest speak of military might. The beads from Europe and cowries from the Indian Ocean were costly imports, so the encrusted surface itself proclaimed the king's reach. In Bamum belief the throne was bound to the authority of the fon, and the Berlin throne remains central to debates over colonial-era restitution.
source: British Museum collections (Mandu Yenu of King Nsangu)

name: Bamileke Elephant Mask
era: Traditional, still used in chiefdom rites
description: Beaded elephant masks of the Cameroon Grassfields are worn by men's societies of the Bamileke and related peoples, who dance them at the funerals of notables, the installation of chiefs, and the festivals of the kwifo, the regulatory society that enforces chiefly authority. The mask takes the shape of an elephant head, with broad flat ears and a central trunk, and is built over carved wood or a cloth and raffia frame before being covered in glass beads in the royal colours of the chiefdom. The elephant, like the leopard, belongs to the forest powers that underwrite Grassfields kingship, and the mask links the wearer, the fon, and the world of the bush spirits. Only society members and people of rank may wear or even touch such masks, which are kept hidden and given offerings in the chiefdom's storehouses. Collections in European and American museums have carried the form worldwide, and Grassfields bead artists continue the tradition today.
source: Museum collections of Cameroon Grassfields royal arts

name: Nkul Slit Gong
description: The nkul is a wooden slit gong of the Beti and related peoples of southern Cameroon, made from a hollowed log with a long longitudinal slit that is beaten with sticks to produce two distinct tones. In forest villages where sound carries poorly, the nkul served as a talking instrument: different rhythms announced deaths, births, hunting results, danger, and the summons to ritual, and a skilled beater could be understood over several kilometres of valley. It also marked the rhythm of communal life, accompanying dances, initiations, and the sessions of the secret societies, and the largest gongs were communal property hung in the meeting house. Slit gongs of the same type are found across Central and West Africa under many names, showing how widespread this early signalling technology became. The nkul remains in use in rural Cameroon, although radio and telephones have taken over most of its message-carrying role.

name: Nkisi Nkondi Power Figure
material: Carved wood, iron blades and nails, mirror, pigment
powers: Held to hunt wrongdoers, seal oaths, and settle disputes; each driven blade records a sworn act.
description: The nkisi nkondi is a power figure of the Kongo people of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a carved wooden human or animal figure studded with nails, blades, and other iron objects. A ritual specialist (nganga) activated the figure to hunt down wrongdoers, witness and seal oaths, settle disputes, and protect homes and villages, and each blade or nail driven into the body recorded one act sworn before it. The figure's aggressive posture, with a raised arm, staring eyes, and a mirror set in the belly, proclaimed its readiness to act, and the nganga called on its spirit to pursue thieves and sorcerers. The most celebrated form is the anthropomorphic 'mangaaka' of the coastal Kongo, commissioned by chiefs for justice-making. When colonial courts suppressed the use of the figures, many were collected by Europeans, and they are now celebrated in museums as masterpieces of Kongo art even as their ritual role faded. The word nkisi itself points to the wider Kongo class of spirit-charged objects.
source: Kongo ritual tradition; museum collections (British Museum, Brooklyn Museum)

name: Lukasa Memory Board
description: The lukasa is a wooden memory board of the Luba peoples of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, its surface covered with beads, shells, and metal pins arranged in clusters that encode historical and ritual knowledge. A member of the Mbudye association, the court's body of historians, reads the board by touch, tracing the beads as a mnemonic that calls forth genealogies, royal protocol, migration legends, and the esoteric teachings of the kingdom. Because each board belonged to a particular specialist and was arranged to fit his memory, no two lukasa are identical, and the objects were kept secret from the uninitiated. The tradition is bound to the founding legends of the Luba state, and the boards are still referenced in the stories of the culture heroes Kalala Ilunga and Mbidi Kiluwe. Scholars such as Mary Nooter Roberts have studied the lukasa as a case of embodied, non-written memory, and the boards are among the best-known objects of Central African court art. Luba historians and diviners continue to use them in their work today.
source: Luba court tradition; scholarly studies (M. Nooter Roberts)

name: Kuba Beaded Cup
material: Wood, glass beads, cowrie shells, brass studs
description: The beaded drinking cups of the Kuba kingdom of the Democratic Republic of the Congo are carved from wood and densely covered with cowrie shells, brass tacks, and patterns of imported glass beads in geometric bands. Owned by kings, titled nobles, and wealthy men, the cups were used in the court ceremonies where palm wine was shared, and they were kept among the treasured possessions of the palace or the lineage house. Some cups take the form of a human head or a pair of feet, while others are plain beakers, and the intricate beadwork set the craftsmen of the royal workshops apart from ordinary potters. In Kuba court culture, drinking vessels were markers of rank, and the most elaborate pieces announced the generosity and wealth of the man who poured from them. The cups entered museum collections during the colonial period, and beaded Kuba cups are now recognised as a high point of African decorative art.

name: Kuba Ndop Royal Figure
description: The ndop is a carved wooden portrait figure of a Kuba king of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, showing the ruler seated cross-legged on a small platform. Each ndop was made for a reigning or remembered king and bears his personal emblem (ibol), a drum, a weapon, or a game board carved beside the seat, while the pattern of scarification on the torso identifies the individual monarch. The figures were kept in the sacred houses of the palace, guarded by the king's titleholders, and were brought out in ceremonies where they stood for the continuity of the throne. Despite the name, the ndop is not a naturalistic likeness but an idealised image of royal authority, and scholars disagree over whether some figures were carved after the king's death as memorials. The oldest surviving examples date to the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and a group of them was carried from the capital during the colonial expeditions before entering the British Museum and other collections. They remain the most celebrated images of Kuba kingship.
source: Kuba royal tradition; museum collections (British Museum)

name: Teke Kidumu Mask
description: The kidumu is a round, flat face mask of the Teke people of the Republic of the Congo, cut from wood and painted with bold geometric patterns in red, white, and black. Worn by the men of the kidumu society at initiations, funerals, and the dances that mark the transfer of authority from one generation to the next, the mask is held before the face horizontally or vertically depending on the region. The painted motifs are not mere decoration: they allude to the sacred knowledge of the group, and elders say the patterns echo the Teke account of creation, in which the world grew from the back of a great turtle. Different mask types correspond to different grades within the society, and the masks are stored in sacred places out of sight of women and the uninitiated. Teke mask-making survives in the republic today, and kidumu masks have become familiar worldwide through museum collections.

name: Chokwe Pwo Mask
material: Carved wood, pigment, fibre and feathers
description: The pwo is the carved female mask of the Chokwe of Angola and neighbouring lands, with a finely finished face, gently closed eyes, and filed or scarified markings on the forehead and cheeks. Danced at the mukanda initiations that turn boys into men and at celebrations of the community, the mask embodies the idealised ancestress, Mwana Pwo, the Young Woman, whose beauty and calm set the standard of Chokwe womanhood. The dancer who wears it takes on the gentle, swaying movements of a woman, while a headdress of fibre and feathers completes the costume. Pwo masks come in pairs with the male cihongo mask of the chief, and both are danced with wit and prestige. Carvers claim to receive guidance in dreams, and each mask is finished with a dark patina meant to evoke the oiled skin of a beautiful woman. Chokwe carving, of which the pwo is the best-known face, has been admired since the first pieces reached Europe.

name: Chokwe Chief's Throne
description: The carved wooden thrones of the Chokwe chiefs of Angola are low seats supported by figural groups, ancestors, rulers, hunters, and scenes of everyday life, that turn each throne into a small chronicle of the chiefdom. The seat and backrest are often studded with brass tacks and worked with openwork motifs, while the supporting figures served as personal emblems of the soba and his lineage. Thrones were made by the chief's carvers and passed down the chiefly line, and a new ruler might commission a throne that linked him to the ancestors shown beneath the seat. In Chokwe court culture the throne was a public statement of the dignity of the soba and the continuity of power, used at audiences and ceremonies. The same woodcarvers made the masks, drums, and staffs of office that completed chiefly regalia. Museum examples from the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries have made the Chokwe throne a celebrated form of Central African royal art.

name: Maasai Nborr Collar
description: The nborr is the flat beaded collar worn by Maasai women and, on ceremonial occasions, by young men (moran) of Kenya and Tanzania. Built on a base of hide or wire and covered with dense rows of tiny glass beads, the collar forms a broad crescent that lies across the chest and shoulders. The colour combinations are not arbitrary: red stands for the cattle that are the heart of Maasai life, white for milk and peace, and the patterns signal the age-set, clan, and status of the wearer. Beaded ornaments are made by women, who learn the craft from their mothers, and whose beadwork circulates in the exchanges that build family alliances. The nborr is worn at dances, initiations, and the celebrations that mark the passage of the age-sets. Maasai beadwork has also become an economic mainstay, with women's cooperatives selling collars and jewellery to the wider market.

name: Maasai Rungu Club
description: The rungu is a short throwing club of the Maasai, a knobbed head on a tapering wooden shaft that herders and warriors carry as they move with their cattle. In the past the rungu was a practical weapon for defending livestock against predators and for settling disputes, thrown with a spin that drove the heavy knob home with force. Today it is still carried, but its main work is ceremonial and social: elders raise the rungu to command attention at meetings, and the club is a badge of authority for spokesmen and age-set leaders. Decorated rungu, carved with rings and bands and sometimes tipped with metal, are made for chiefs and for the tourist market. The word has passed into the region's popular culture, and the rungu remains the most recognisable symbol of Maasai leadership.

name: Maasai Shuka Cloth
era: Contemporary, evolving from traditional hide cloth
description: The shuka is the checked cloth, usually in shades of red, that Maasai wrap around the body as a toga-like garment, a dress so distinctive it has become the visual signature of the Maasai in Kenya and Tanzania. Red is the colour of cattle blood and of the warrior ideal, and the bold plaid stands out in the savannah where the herds graze. The shuka replaced the older dress of hides and skins during the twentieth century, when imported cotton cloth spread through the region, and its adoption shows how a modern commodity was absorbed into Maasai identity. Different communities favour different colour families, and the way the cloth is folded and worn, over one shoulder, around the waist, or across the mouth of a herder sheltering from dust, varies with occasion and age-set. Factories in the region now print shuka cloth in bulk, and the checked patterns are also worn far beyond the Maasai as a mark of East African style.

name: Ngoma Drum (Swahili Coast)
description: The ngoma is the wooden drum of the Swahili coast of Tanzania and Kenya, built as a barrel or goblet with a hide head and played in the ensembles that accompany weddings, dances, and life-cycle rites. In Swahili the word ngoma covers drum, dance, and festivity together, and the drumming groups of the coast keep a repertory of named rhythms passed down through families. Ngoma also reaches into the spirit world: in the ceremonies of the pepo, the capricious spirits of the coast, drumming summons the spirits so that they may be spoken to and soothed, and drummers are chosen for their knowledge of the right rhythm for each spirit. Coastal ensembles combine drums of several sizes and pitches, and the master drummer leads with improvised phrases while the group holds the pattern. The tradition is alive today in the taarab and dansi scenes as well as in the village ceremonies where the drums still call the community together.

name: Makonde Shetani Figure
description: The shetani carvings of the Makonde are dark hardwood figures of contorted, expressive spirits, carved from the ebony-like mpingo of the Tanzanian and Mozambican coast. Beginning in the 1950s, carvers turned from ancestor figures to the shetani, capricious bush and ancestral spirits, twisting human and animal forms into elongated, agonised, or playful shapes that seem to catch a spirit mid-transformation. Each carving is original, the forms said to be revealed to the carver in dreams, and the pieces are exhibited as art as much as ritual objects. The word shetani, from the Arabic for 'evil spirit', entered Swahili through Islam, but the figures draw on older Makonde beliefs about the dark forest and its inhabitants. Shetani carving has become one of the most recognisable genres of contemporary African art, sold from Dar es Salaam to international galleries. The tradition also carries the older meaning of the spirits themselves, who are remembered as crowding the Makonde homeland on both sides of the border.

name: Zanzibar Dhow
description: The dhow (jahazi) of Zanzibar is a lateen-sailed wooden vessel built on the Swahili coast for fishing, cargo, and the trade that rode the monsoons across the Indian Ocean. Hulls were traditionally sewn with coconut-coir fibre and caulked, and the ships carried ivory, cloves, mangrove poles, and grain between East Africa, Arabia, and India. The pattern of the monsoons set the rhythm of the whole coast: dhows sailed out on the kusi winds and returned with the kaskazi, and captains timed their passages by the stars. Seafaring was wrapped in maritime belief, and sailors made offerings and prayers to win the favour of the pepo, the sea spirits who were believed to command wind and water. The same trade carried the brasswork, textiles, and coral-stone architecture that shaped the coastal towns. Today traditional dhows still fish the Zanzibar channel, and the wooden dhow industry survives alongside modern vessels.

name: Buganda Royal Drum (Mujaguzo)
description: The mujaguzo are the royal drums of the Buganda kingdom of Uganda, a set of tuned drums kept in a sacred drum house and regarded as the spiritual king of the kingdom. Ganda tradition holds that Buganda has two rulers, the human kabaka and the drums, which never die, and the drums are sounded to announce the birth of a prince, the death of a kabaka, the call to war, and the great ceremonies of state. The principal drum, Kawulugumu, is the 'king among drums', and at a coronation the new kabaka must first visit the drum house, tighten its hide, and strike it to take up his rule; its companion Namanyonyi is spoken of as its wife. The drums are kept suspended above the ground and are smeared with ghee and beer in ritual care, guarded by custodians of the Butiko clan. When the kingdom was abolished in 1966 the drums were hidden away and survived, and they were brought out again for the coronation of 1993. The royal drum tradition remains a living institution of the kabaka's court.

name: Baganda Barkcloth (Olubugo)
material: Beaten inner bark of the mutuba fig tree
description: Olubugo is the barkcloth of the Baganda of Uganda, made by stripping the inner bark of the mutuba fig tree and beating it with wooden mallets until it becomes a soft, pliable, chestnut-brown textile. The craft is usually practised by men, who peel the bark in the wet season and beat it on a log, folding and turning the sheet until it reaches the desired fineness, and a single tree can be harvested again and again. In the Buganda kingdom, barkcloth was the dress of kings and chiefs, worn in layers that grew thicker with rank, and it was also used in burial, wrapping the dead and lining the royal tombs of Kasubi. Because it belonged to the court and the ancestors, the cloth carries sacred associations, and it is still worn and laid out at funerals and important rituals. UNESCO inscribed Baganda barkcloth-making on the list of intangible cultural heritage in 2005, and makers in the Kampala region produce cloth for ceremony and for the contemporary art and fashion markets alike.
source: Ganda barkcloth tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

name: Ethiopian Processional Cross
description: Ethiopian processional crosses are tall brass, silver, or bronze crosses carried on staffs before the clergy during the liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Each cross is unique, built from a dense tracery of openwork that varies with the workshop and the region; the arms are set in a frame that may be square, round, or diamond-shaped, and the patterns are filled with small figurative and geometric motifs. The cross is both instrument and image: it is held over the congregation as a blessing, kissed by the faithful, and its openwork is understood to evoke the Tree of Life and the victory of Christ. Processional crosses accompany the tabot at outdoor festivals such as the Meskel finding of the True Cross, when the square cross itself stands at the centre of the bonfire ceremony. Silver crosses were made for the great monasteries of Lalibela and Axum, while brass crosses were the common liturgical object of every church. Related hand crosses, carried by every priest, share the same design language.

name: Jebena Coffee Pot
description: The jebena is the round, clay coffee pot of Ethiopia, with a narrow neck, a round belly, and a small spout, fired without glaze and used in the country's coffee ceremony (bunna). In the ceremony, green beans are roasted in a pan over coals, ground, and boiled three times in the jebena, and the pot sits on a bed of fresh grass while incense burns beside it. The first brew, abol, is the strongest and most honoured; the second and third rounds, tona and baraka, follow as the gathering lingers. Pouring from the high-necked pot without spilling is a skill, and the tiny cups are filled from a single unbroken stream. The jebena is central to hospitality: hosting the ceremony is a daily ritual of friendship and community, and the coffee is shared with anyone who arrives. Modern jebena are also made in metal and glazed ceramic, but the hand-built clay pot remains the heart of the tradition.

name: Ethiopian Ketab Protective Scroll
material: Parchment, ink, leather or cloth cover
powers: Worn or hung to ward off evil spirits, illness, and the harm attributed to buda.
description: Ketab are protective prayer scrolls of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, strips of parchment inscribed with prayers, sacred names, and devotional images, then rolled and worn or hung as amulets. They are written by debtera, the church's trained scholars, and by diviners, who combine liturgical texts with protective formulae in Ge'ez. The scrolls guard the wearer against evil spirits, illness, the evil eye, and the harm that is believed to come from buda, the people accused of possessing the evil eye. A scroll's shape follows its purpose: some are narrow strips folded into a leather case for wearing round the neck, while others are long, illustrated rolls made for the sick to keep at home. The images, crosses, eyes, saints, and the Archangel Michael on his horse, echo church painting in miniature. Ketab are still commissioned today, keeping alive a manuscript tradition that reaches back centuries.
source: Ethiopian magical scroll tradition; scholarly studies (J. Mercier)

name: Kalinga Royal Drum
description: The Kalinga was the most sacred drum of the Rwandan court, the principal of the four royal drums that together stood for the kingship of the mwami. Kept in a sacred house where a fire burned day and night, the drum was never allowed to touch the ground and was rubbed with bull's blood and herbs to renew its power. According to oral tradition the Kalinga reached the court with the seventeenth-century king Ruganzu II Ndori, and it travelled with the king on campaign, acquiring personal names as if it were a living ruler. The Kalinga stood for the male principle and the king, its companion drum for the queen mother, and Rwandans said 'he is king who has the drums': beating it at coronations, harvests, and victories affirmed the dynasty's authority. After the monarchy was abolished in the early 1960s the royal drums vanished from public sight, and no trace of the originals has been found, though the drums live on in the country's drumming tradition and in the re-created court dances of the Intore.

name: Somali Dabqaad Incense Burner
description: The dabqaad is the incense burner of Somali homes, a small clay or soapstone bowl raised on short legs and covered by a perforated lid from which the smoke of frankincense and myrrh rises. Somalia sits at the eastern end of the ancient incense lands, and the gums burned in the dabqaad were the same resins traded to Egypt, Rome, and the Gulf for thousands of years. In daily use the burner perfumes the house, and a lit dabqaad is placed near the door to welcome guests, to scent the rooms after cooking, and to sweeten the air at weddings and religious gatherings. The perforated lid lets the smoke rise in a fine plume, and the burner is carried from room to room by the women of the household. The dabqaad keeps the Horn of Africa's incense culture alive in domestic form, linking modern Somali life to one of the oldest trades in the world.

name: Mahafaly Aloalo Funerary Post
description: The aloalo are the carved funerary posts of the Mahafaly people of southwestern Madagascar, tall wooden stelae that stand on the stone tombs of chiefs and wealthy families. The name comes from alo, 'intermediary' or 'messenger', and the posts are believed to help the dead cross into the community of the ancestors. A classic aloalo rises through a column of openwork geometric shapes, crescents and circles often read as the phases of the moon, to a finial carved as a human figure, a zebu, or a bird such as the cattle egret, while the horns of zebu sacrificed at the funeral are arranged at the tomb's base. The zebu, the measure of wealth in the region, is carved again and again, and recent aloalo add motifs such as bicycles, aeroplanes, and scenes from the deceased's life. Only commissioned carvers make aloalo, which were once the right of royalty alone. The posts have become an emblem of Madagascar, and the Mahafaly tomb country is a candidate for the World Heritage list.

name: Zulu Iziqu Necklace
material: Carved wood or bone blocks, fibre
description: The iziqu is the necklace of a Zulu warrior, made of carved wooden beads strung on a cord and worn across the chest as a mark of valour. After a king recognised a man for bravery in battle, the warrior was permitted to carve and string the necklace himself, usually from the wood of the thorn tree, and each row was said to record a heroic deed; Maclean, who saw the court of Shaka in 1825, described the necklaces as orders of merit conferred by the king's own hand. The iziqu was the second-highest decoration of the Zulu army after the brass armband (ingxotha), and the carved beads could be combined with bone, horn, and skin in protective war charms. The most famous string, the long wooden necklace of King Dinizulu, was taken by Robert Baden-Powell in 1888 and inspired the wooden beads of the Scout Wood Badge. A giant bronze iziqu crowns the Isandlwana monument honouring the Zulu army of 1879. Today the iziqu is remembered as one of the few personal honours a common warrior could win.

name: Zulu Iwisa Knobkerrie
description: The iwisa, often called the knobkerrie, is a Zulu club made from a single piece of hardwood, with a heavy round knob at the top of a straight or slightly curved handle. It was a close-combat weapon of the Zulu army, carried beside the spear and thrown or swung in the close fights of the impi, and it remained a warrior's constant companion when herding and walking. In peacetime the iwisa became a staff of rank: chiefs, headmen, and later officials carried finely carved examples, and the club is still raised in the air at ceremonies, weddings, and political gatherings as a gesture of authority. Craftsmen shaped the knob and handle with an adze and burnished them smooth, and the best pieces are polished to a deep shine. The knobkerrie has spread beyond the Zulu, serving as the famous weapon and walking stick of southern African leadership.

name: Zulu Ukhamba Beer Pot
description: The ukhamba is the clay beer pot of the Zulu, a round, low-necked vessel fired from local clay and used to brew and serve utshwala, the sorghum beer at the centre of Zulu hospitality. Beer is not everyday drink but the medium of ceremony: it is brewed by women, offered to the ancestors at the start of every gathering, and shared at marriages, funerals, and the community work-parties that bind homesteads together. The pot's shape is practical, the round belly holding the fermenting beer and the narrow mouth keeping it clean, and the clay keeps the beer cool. Well-made ukhamba are prized, and a woman's skill at brewing and presenting beer is a matter of family pride. Decorated pots, incised with patterns or fitted with beadwork covers, are made for important occasions, and Zulu pottery has been collected and exhibited as art. The ukhamba remains in daily use in KwaZulu-Natal alongside the woven beer-strainers and calabashes that complete the brewing set.

name: Xhosa Beadwork
description: Xhosa beadwork of South Africa is made with imported glass beads sewn onto leather, cotton, or cloth supports to create necklaces, aprons, headdresses, and panels of dress worn at the great passages of life. At initiation, the beads speak: the colours and patterns worn by a young man in the circumcision school, and by the women who celebrate his return, carry coded messages of love, status, and clan that are meant to be read by the initiated. Married women wear beadwork that records their lineage and their husband's house, while older styles of white and blue bands gave way to the bright colour families of the modern era. Beadwork was a woman's art, taught by mothers and grandmothers, and its patterns changed with fashion while keeping their social grammar. Today Xhosa beadwork is worn at weddings, initiation feasts, and church festivals, and the beaded garments of the Red Xhosa communities of the Eastern Cape remain the most photographed tradition. Cooperatives and designers now sell Xhosa beadwork across South Africa and abroad.

name: Mbira Dzavadzimu
description: The mbira dzavadzimu is the lamellophone of the Shona people of Zimbabwe, a wooden soundboard fitted with rows of metal keys and placed over a gourd resonator that buzzes with shells, bottle caps, or other rattling matter. Its name means 'mbira of the ancestor spirits', and it is played at the bira ceremonies where the spirits of the departed are called to advise the living. The interlocking patterns of the mbira weave around the singing and clapping of the assembly, and the buzzing, layered sound is thought to attract the spirits so that they can speak through a medium. The instrument is learned by hand within Shona families, and certain mbira pieces are held by specific lineages as inherited property. After independence the mbira became a national emblem of Zimbabwe, and its sound now opens radio broadcasts and accompanies church hymns. The instrument's deep, hypnotic cycles have also carried it into world music through Zimbabwean players and teachers.

name: Soapstone Bird of Great Zimbabwe
description: The soapstone birds of Great Zimbabwe are carved birds about 40 centimetres tall, with human lips, folded wings, and feet that grip the columns on which they once stood within the ruined stone city. Eight are known, six large and two small, and they are believed to have been royal emblems of the Shona state that built the city between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, possibly representations of the bateleur eagle, the fish eagle, or a spirit bird of kingship. The birds probably crowned the walls and monoliths of the royal enclosure, marking the authority of the ruler, and the city itself gave its name to modern Zimbabwe. In the 1890s the carvings were hacked from their columns and carried to South Africa, where one passed into the hands of Cecil Rhodes; five birds were returned in 1981 and the last in 2026, ending more than a century of exile. The bird was adopted as Zimbabwe's national symbol in 1924 and appears on the flag, the coat of arms, and the country's coins.
source: Archaeological finds at Great Zimbabwe; UNESCO World Heritage

name: Chipendani Mouth Bow
description: The chipendani is a mouth bow of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a curved wooden stave with a single fibre or wire string, held against the open mouth and plucked so that the mouth shapes the tone. Because the cavity of the mouth acts as a resonator, the player can vary pitch and timbre while the string keeps up a light, rhythmic pattern. It is above all an instrument of herders and young men, who play it alone in the fields to pass the hours, to court, and to accompany themselves while singing. The chipendani is small and portable, carried in the hand or tucked in the belt, and its soft sound suits the quiet company of cattle rather than the crowd. Related mouth bows appear across southern Africa under different names. Although the mbira overshadowed it in the modern Shona music revival, the chipendani is still heard in the countryside and is taught in some schools and cultural programmes.

name: Lozi Royal Barge
description: The Lozi royal barge, the nalikwanda, is the great wooden vessel that carries the Litunga, the king of the Lozi people of western Zambia, at the Kuomboka ceremony. When the annual floods rise on the Zambezi, the king leaves the lowland palace and is paddled in procession to higher ground, the barge covered with an immense shroud of black-and-white cloth and surrounded by dozens of escort boats. The crossing is the climax of Kuomboka, a pageant that renews the bond between the king and the waters that shape Lozi life, and the barge's heavy, deliberate movement through the flood is timed to the songs of its rowers. The nalikwanda is built of timber by Lozi boatbuilders, and a new barge is commissioned when the old one fails. Kuomboka, whose name means 'to get out of the water', draws thousands of spectators each year. The barge is the central object of the most famous river festival in southern Africa.

name: Gule Wamkulu Mask
description: The gule wamkulu masks of the Chewa of Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique are carved wooden face masks worn by the dancers of the Nyau society, whose great dance of the same name is performed at initiations, funerals, and the memorials of the dead. Nyau means 'the big dance' or 'the dance of the spirits', and the masked dancers embody the ancestors, the animals of the bush, and the forces of the forest, revealing their meanings only to initiates. Each mask has a name and a character, the gentle, the comic, the terrible, and the dancer becomes the spirit while he wears it, speaking in its voice. The Nyau society, open only to initiated men, holds the history and the law of the Chewa, and the masks are stored in hidden groves away from women and strangers. UNESCO inscribed the gule wamkulu on the intangible heritage list in 2005. The tradition is still danced with force in the villages of the Chewa heartland.
source: Chewa Nyau tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
